case.title: A Mathematical Theory of Communication (C. E. Shannon, 1948), Section 6 Choice, Uncertainty and Entropy
case.excerpt: 6. Choice, Uncertainty and Entropy. Suppose we have a set of possible events whose probabilities of occurrence are p_1, p_2, ..., p_n. These probabilities are known but that is all we know concerning which event will occur. Can we find a measure of how much "choice" is involved in the selection of the event, or of how uncertain we are of the outcome? If there is such a measure, say H(p_1, p_2, ..., p_n), it is reasonable to require of it the following properties: (1) H should be continuous in the p_i. (2) If all the p_i are equal, p_i = 1/n, then H should be a monotonic increasing function of n: with equally likely events there is more choice, or uncertainty, when there are more possible events. (3) If a choice be broken down into two successive choices, the original H should be the weighted sum of the individual values of H. Theorem 2: The only H satisfying the three above assumptions is of the form H = -K sum_{i=1}^{n} p_i log p_i, where K is a positive constant (it merely amounts to a choice of a unit of measure). Quantities of the form H = -sum p_i log p_i play a central role in information theory as measures of information, choice and uncertainty, and will be recognized as the entropy of statistical mechanics. With logarithms to the base 2, the unit is the bit. Properties of H: (1) H = 0 if and only if all the p_i but one are zero, this one having the value unity; thus only when we are certain of the outcome does H vanish, otherwise H is positive. (2) For a given n, H is a maximum and equal to log n when all the p_i are equal (i.e., 1/n); this is also intuitively the most uncertain situation. For two possibilities with probabilities p and q = 1 - p, H = -(p log p + q log q), which is plotted as a function of p in Fig. 7.
case.focus: Explain discrete entropy (Section 6, H = -sum p_i log2 p_i) using a small probability distribution. Let the learner change the distribution and the number of outcomes. Show probabilities, individual contributions, and total entropy in bits. Compare a certain outcome with equally likely outcomes. Check that certainty gives zero bits and four equally likely outcomes give two bits; handle zero probabilities correctly.
case.audience: Engineering undergraduate who knows basic probability and logarithms but has not studied information theory.

plan.concept: Discrete entropy H = -sum p_i log2 p_i as a measure of choice/uncertainty, its properties (H=0 iff certain, H=log2 n when uniform), and correct handling of zero probabilities.

spec.title: Entropy: How Much Choice Is in a Distribution?
spec.hook: Shannon asked how to measure the 'choice' in a set of probabilities. Move the probabilities and the number of outcomes, and watch the entropy in bits respond.
spec.idea:
Suppose a random experiment has $n$ possible outcomes with probabilities $p_1,\dots,p_n$ that sum to 1. Shannon wanted a number $H(p_1,\dots,p_n)$ that measures how uncertain we are about the outcome. He required three things: $H$ is continuous in the $p_i$; if all outcomes are equally likely then $H$ increases with $n$; and splitting a choice into two stages makes $H$ the weighted sum of the parts.

Theorem 2 says the only function satisfying these is $H = -K\sum_i p_i \log p_i$. Choosing base-2 logarithms and $K=1$ makes the unit the **bit**. Each term $-p_i\log_2 p_i$ is that outcome's contribution: an outcome with tiny probability contributes little because it rarely happens, and an outcome with probability near 1 also contributes little because it is nearly certain.

Two properties follow directly. If one outcome has probability 1 and the rest are 0, every term is 0, so $H=0$: certainty means no uncertainty. If all $n$ outcomes are equally likely, $p_i=1/n$, then $H=\log_2 n$, the largest possible value for that $n$.

Zero probabilities need care: $\log_2 0$ is undefined, but $p\log_2 p \to 0$ as $p\to 0^+$, so the convention is that a zero-probability outcome contributes exactly 0 to $H$.
spec.why: Entropy is the foundation of information theory, data compression, and channel capacity. Seeing it as a sum of per-outcome contributions makes clear why uniform distributions carry the most uncertainty and why certainty carries none.

equations.caption: Theorem 2: the unique measure satisfying Shannon's three requirements; $K$ is a positive constant fixing the unit.
With base-2 logarithms and $K=1$, the unit is the bit.
Property (2): for fixed $n$, $H$ is maximized and equals $\log_2 n$ when all outcomes are equally likely.
Property (1): a zero-probability outcome contributes nothing; $H=0$ iff one outcome has probability 1.

A contribution bar of zero height means that outcome adds no uncertainty.

explorations.title: Certainty versus equally likely
explorations.change: Turn on 'Force equally likely', then turn it off and drag $p_1$ back toward 1.
explorations.observe: With $p=(1,0,0,0)$ the total entropy reads 0 bits and all contribution bars vanish. With the toggle on, $p=(0.25,0.25,0.25,0.25)$ and the total reads 2 bits, matching $\log_2 4$.
explorations.why: A certain outcome has $p\log_2 p = 0$ for every term, so $H=0$. Equal probabilities give each term $0.25\times 2 = 0.5$, and four of them sum to 2.

explorations.title: More outcomes, more uncertainty
explorations.change: Increase $n$ from 2 to 6 with the uniform toggle on.
explorations.observe: The total entropy rises from 1 bit at $n=2$ to about 2.585 bits at $n=6$, tracking $\log_2 n$; the ceiling line moves up too.
explorations.why: Property (2): with equally likely events, $H=\log_2 n$ is monotonic increasing in $n$, so more possible events means more choice.

pitfall.title: Zero probability is not an error
pitfall.text: A zero-probability outcome makes $\log_2 0$ undefined, but the limit $p\log_2 p \to 0$ as $p\to 0^+$ means its contribution is exactly 0. The page applies this convention, so setting a slider to 0 never produces NaN or Infinity.

grounding.paper: A Mathematical Theory of Communication (C. E. Shannon, 1948)
grounding.section: Section 6, Choice, Uncertainty and Entropy; Theorem 2 and the properties of H
from_source: Shannon requires H to be continuous in the p_i, monotonic increasing in n when all p_i are equal, and additive when a choice is broken into successive choices.
Theorem 2: the only H satisfying these is H = -K sum p_i log p_i, with K a positive constant fixing the unit.
With logarithms to base 2 the unit is the bit.
Property (1): H = 0 if and only if all p_i but one are zero, that one having value unity.
Property (2): for a given n, H is maximum and equal to log n when all p_i are equal to 1/n.
For two possibilities with probabilities p and q = 1-p, H = -(p log p + q log q).
our_additions: The interactive sliders, the bar/contribution visual, and the two-outcome curve are our teaching aids, not figures from the paper.
The convention that a zero-probability term contributes 0 is the standard limit of p log p as p -> 0.
The 'uniform' toggle and the two-outcome select are convenience controls we added.
grounding.disclaimer: This is a toy illustration of the entropy formula on small hand-set distributions. It does not reproduce any experiment or numerical result from Shannon's paper.
